prompt: On iOS, how does a `Form` lay out the controls inside it?
hint: Think of the Settings app.

choices.text: As aligned vertical stacks, with a colon after each label
choices.why: That is how the same code looks on macOS, according to Apple's documentation for `Form`.

choices.text: As a grouped list, one group per section
choices.why: Right: each `Section` is one rounded group with its heading over it.

choices.text: As a grid, two controls to a row
choices.why: A `Form` stacks its rows; a grid is a different container.

choices.text: Exactly as a `VStack` would, with no styling
choices.why: The point of `Form` is the platform's own styling for data entry.

prompt: The course picker's selection is `String?`. What is the first row, `Text("Choose one")`, tagged with?
hint: It stands for the draft having no course yet.

choices.text: An empty string, `""`
choices.why: An empty string would be a course id; the draft's "no course" is `nil`.

choices.text: `String?.none`, which is `nil`
choices.why: Right: it matches `courseID == nil`, which `problems` reports as `noCourse`.

choices.text: Nothing, since the first row of a picker is its label
choices.why: The label is the picker's first argument, `"Course"`.

choices.text: The id of the first course in the list
choices.why: Then the form would start with a course chosen for the person.

prompt: Why does the Add button call `draft.session(…)` instead of building a `StudySession` itself?
hint: Where can the rules be tested without a screen?

choices.text: The rules live in the package, tested anywhere and shared
choices.why: Right. The screen decides nothing about validity, so section 04's tests cover every rule.

choices.text: SwiftUI views are not allowed to create structs
choices.why: A view can create any value; the reason is where the rules can be tested.

choices.text: `StudySession` has no public initialiser
choices.why: It does: lesson 1 made its `init` public.

choices.text: It makes the button respond faster when tapped
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

prompt: A field is `TextField("Minutes", value: $minutes, format: .number)`, `minutes` is 30, and somebody types `forty`. What does `minutes` hold?
hint: Read Apple's sentence about a conversion that fails.

choices.text: 0, because `forty` is not a number
choices.why: Nothing sets it to zero: a failed conversion leaves the binding as it was.

choices.text: `nil`, until a valid number is typed
choices.why: `minutes` is an `Int`, which cannot be `nil`.

choices.text: Still 30, while the field shows `forty`
choices.why: Right, and that gap between the screen and the model is why the planner binds to text.

choices.text: 40, since the format style reads words in English
choices.why: A number format reads digits in the locale's form, not spelled-out words.

prompt: The minutes field has `.keyboardType(.numberPad)`. Why does the draft still check for `minutesNotWhole`?
hint: What else can put text into a field?

choices.text: The number pad has a decimal key on every iPhone
choices.why: The reason is broader: the keypad is not the only way text arrives.

choices.text: A hardware keyboard or a paste still types letters
choices.why: Right: a keyboard type is a convenience, and the draft is the check.

choices.text: `keyboardType` is ignored inside a `Form`
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation says so; the modifier applies in a form.

choices.text: To pass App Store review, which demands it
choices.why: Review does not read the validation; people do.

prompt: Match each modifier to what it changes about the minutes field.
hint: None of them changes what the field holds.

pairs.right: Which keys the software keyboard shows
Whether a word is proposed as you type
The word on the return key
Which value focus state takes in this field

right_distractors: Rejects anything that is not a digit

prompt: Your settings screen has a font-size field from 10 to 30, defaulting to 17. Is a `TextField(value:format:)` reasonable there?
hint: The section names when snapping back to the last valid value is acceptable.

choices.text: No: a number field loses what is typed, in any screen
choices.why: The section says it is acceptable for a value with a sensible fallback.

choices.text: Yes: there is a safe value to snap back to
choices.why: Right. The cost is a silent snap-back, which matters for a session and hardly for a font size.

choices.text: Yes, because a format style refuses numbers outside 10 to 30
choices.why: A format style converts text; it knows nothing of a range.

choices.text: No, because format styles only exist on macOS
choices.why: They exist in Foundation on every platform, iOS included.

prompt: What does `SessionDraft.problems` return for a draft with no course and the minutes `lots`?
hint: A test in section 04 compares exactly this.

choices.text: `[.noCourse]`, because it stops at the first problem
choices.why: It collects every problem; stopping at the first is what the test is there to prevent.

choices.text: `[.noCourse, .minutesNotWhole("lots")]`
choices.why: Right: both, in the order the form shows the fields.

choices.text: `[.minutesNotWhole("lots")]`
choices.why: The missing course is a problem too.

choices.text: A sentence: "Choose a course and enter minutes"
choices.why: Problems are values; the words are the form's.

prompt: Why are the draft's problems values like `.minutesOutOfRange(600)` rather than sentences?
hint: Who reads the words, and in which language?

choices.text: Enums take less memory than strings
choices.why: Memory is not the reason; the words belong to the screen and its language.

choices.text: Swift does not allow a `String` in an `Equatable` type
choices.why: It does; `String` is `Equatable`.

choices.text: So the screen words them in the person's language and tests name the case
choices.why: Right. A sentence would tie the rule to English and make tests compare prose.

choices.text: VoiceOver reads only enum values aloud
choices.why: VoiceOver reads the text on the screen, which the form writes.

prompt: How many tests did `swift test` pass in this lesson's package?
hint: Lesson 1's and this lesson's together.

prompt: The planner accepts between 5 and ___ minutes for one session.
hint: Eight hours.

prompt: `draft` printed `instant 2026-10-22 02:30:00 +0000` for a moment picked as 23:30 on the 21st in São Paulo. Why the 22nd?
hint: `print` shows a `Date` in one fixed zone.

choices.text: The picker added three hours by mistake
choices.why: Nothing was added: it is the same instant, written in UTC.

choices.text: `print` writes the instant in UTC, three hours ahead
choices.why: Right. São Paulo is UTC−3, so 23:30 there is 02:30 the next day in UTC.

choices.text: The machine's clock was set to the wrong day
choices.why: The program never reads the clock; the instant is written in it.

choices.text: Daylight saving time moved it an hour, twice
choices.why: São Paulo has no daylight saving time in 2026; the offset is three hours.

prompt: A tester in São Paulo adds sessions at lunchtime and every day is right; a student who studies at night files sessions under the next day. What is wrong?
hint: Lunchtime in São Paulo is the same day in UTC.

choices.text: The minutes field rounds values up after 21:00
choices.why: Minutes are never rounded, and they are not dates.

choices.text: `mondayOf` uses UTC, so it must use the phone's zone
choices.why: `mondayOf` reads a day that is already text, where UTC is right; the bug is earlier.

choices.text: The picked instant becomes a day in UTC, not the person's calendar
choices.why: Right. After 21:00 in São Paulo it is already tomorrow in UTC, which is why lunchtime tests pass.

choices.text: The DatePicker shows the time, which confuses it
choices.why: `displayedComponents: .date` hides the time; the instant is still there either way.

prompt: Which typed value does the draft report as `noMinutes` rather than `minutesNotWhole`?
hint: The output's empty line.

choices.text: `forty`
choices.why: A word is `minutesNotWhole`.

choices.text: An empty field
choices.why: Right: "enter the minutes" is kinder than "not a number" to somebody who has not typed yet.

choices.text: `1.5`, a decimal
choices.why: `Int` cannot read it, so it is `minutesNotWhole("1.5")`.

choices.text: `0`, which is a number of nothing
choices.why: Zero is a number, out of range: `minutesOutOfRange(0)`.

prompt: Why does the draft refuse `1.5` instead of rounding it to 2?
hint: What did the person probably mean?

choices.text: They probably meant hours, and 2 minutes would be wrong
choices.why: Right: refusing asks the person; rounding guesses, badly.

choices.text: `Int` rounds towards zero, which gives 1, and the draft wants 2
choices.why: `Int("1.5")` gives `nil`; it does not round at all.

choices.text: Decimals are forbidden in every `TextField` on iOS
choices.why: A text field holds any text; the rule is the draft's.

choices.text: Two minutes is under the planner's floor of five
choices.why: True, but the draft never gets that far: `1.5` is refused as not whole.

prompt: What is wrong with putting `.disabled(!draft.problems.isEmpty)` on the Add button?
hint: What does a grey button say?

choices.text: It stops the form from compiling
choices.why: It compiles and works; the problem is what the person is told.

choices.text: A disabled button can still be tapped
choices.why: It cannot; that is what disabled means.

choices.text: It says no and never says why
choices.why: Right. The planner keeps Add enabled and shows the problems when it is tapped.

choices.text: `problems` is too slow to compute on every keystroke
choices.why: It is a few comparisons on a short string.

prompt: In the planner's form, what does setting `focused = nil` do?
hint: Apple's documentation for `FocusState` says it.

choices.text: Moves focus back to the first field
choices.why: That would be setting it to that field's value.

choices.text: Takes focus off every field, so the keyboard goes away
choices.why: Right: it is the whole implementation of the Done button.

choices.text: Clears the text in the focused field
choices.why: Focus is about where typing goes, not what was typed.

choices.text: Disables the fields until Add is tapped
choices.why: Nothing is disabled; focus simply leaves.

prompt: `minutesMessage` returns `LocalizedStringKey?`. What would change if it returned `String?` and nothing else changed?
hint: How does `Text` treat a variable string?

choices.text: Nothing, since both are text
choices.why: `Text` treats them differently: only a key is looked up in the catalogue.

choices.text: It would not compile, since `Text` takes no `String`
choices.why: `Text` has an initialiser for a string value; it shows it verbatim.

choices.text: A Portuguese phone would see the English message
choices.why: Right: a `String` variable is shown verbatim, with no lookup in the string catalogue.

choices.text: VoiceOver would stop reading the message aloud
choices.why: VoiceOver reads whatever text is shown, localised or not.

prompt: Why does the minutes field need a Done button in a `.keyboard` toolbar?
hint: Look at the keys the number pad has.

choices.text: `.onSubmit` is not allowed on a number field
choices.why: It is allowed; it simply has no return key to fire it.

choices.text: The number pad has no return key
choices.why: Right, so a person who typed 45 had nothing to press.

choices.text: App Store review rejects a form with no Done button
choices.why: The reason is the person typing, not review.

choices.text: The keyboard toolbar is where Add has to go
choices.why: Add stays in the navigation bar; Done goes above the keyboard.

prompt: What does SwiftUI treat the software keyboard as, so that content avoids it?
hint: It is listed with the status bar and the home indicator.

choices.text: A sheet presented over the screen
choices.why: A sheet is a presentation; the keyboard is a region content is laid out around.

choices.text: An overlay the app has to measure itself
choices.why: SwiftUI does that for you; the app writes no code for it.

choices.text: Part of the safe area
choices.why: Right: `SafeAreaRegions` has a `keyboard` region, and `.ignoresSafeArea(.keyboard)` opts out of it.

choices.text: A toolbar placement at the bottom
choices.why: `.keyboard` is also a toolbar placement, but that is for items above the keyboard.

prompt: Since iOS 16, what does scrolling a `Form` do to the keyboard, by default?
hint: Apple's documentation for `scrollDismissesKeyboard(_:)` gives it.

choices.text: It dismisses it when the scroll begins
choices.why: Right; only a `TextEditor` defaults to interactive.

choices.text: Nothing: it stays until Done is tapped
choices.why: That is the `.never` mode, which has to be asked for.

choices.text: It follows the finger down, interactively, as in Messages
choices.why: That is the default for a `TextEditor` only.

choices.text: It moves the focus to the next field
choices.why: Scrolling does not move focus.

prompt: Put what happens in order, from typing `forty` to a session being added.

items: The person types `forty` in the minutes field

prompt: Which of these are decided by the package, and so held by `swift test` on Linux? Choose all that apply.
hint: The screen decides where focus goes; the draft decides what is valid.

choices.text: That ` 45 ` is accepted as 45 minutes
choices.why: Yes: the draft trims, and a test pins it.

choices.text: That focus moves to the minutes after a failed Add
choices.why: No: that is `SessionForm`'s, checked by UI tests on a Mac.

choices.text: That a moment at 23:30 in São Paulo is the 21st
choices.why: Yes: `day(of:in:)` is in the package and tested.

choices.text: That the keyboard goes away when Done is tapped
choices.why: No: that is focus state on the screen.
